answer:
Split the requirement in two, because the CRM's own boundary runs straight through it.

WHAT BELONGS IN THE FILE'S DOCUMENTED HISTORY (model it in the CRM)

1. The disposal-review decision, once taken, is an event with a date and a responsible person, and the CRM models it precisely. Use E17 Type Assignment (a subclass of E13 Attribute Assignment): P41 classified -> the file, P42 assigned -> an E55 Type from a small controlled list ('destroy', 'retain permanently'), P14 carried out by -> the records officer (E39), P4 has time-span -> the date the review actually took place. E17's scope note is written for exactly this situation: it 'allows for the documentation of the context of classification acts in cases where the value of the classification depends on the personal opinion of the classifier, and the date that the classification was made'. A curator's appraisal judgement is that case verbatim.

This also satisfies the CRM's Monotonicity principle. A bare 'retention status' field on the file is a current-state property; the specification says of such properties that this information is non-monotonic, i.e. it requires deletion when the state changes, and that the CRM 'always gives priority to modelling properties as time-neutral, and rather representing changes by events'. Fifteen-year review cycles mean the status will be revisited; a dated E17 per review accumulates without contradiction, whereas a status field has to be overwritten and the earlier decision is lost.

2. The retention schedule itself is E29 Design or Procedure - 'documented plans for the execution of actions in order to achieve a result of a specific quality, form, or contents'. Attach it to each review with P33 used specific technique (E7 -> E29), whose scope note explicitly anticipates 'intervention plans for conservation' as the paradigm case. That records which schedule, and which version of it, governed a given decision - which is the audit trail an archive actually needs.

3. The ground of the decision. Record the two-valued distinction as an E55 Type reached by P21 had general purpose on the review ('statutory retention' vs 'retention for historical value'); the CRM's About Types section is explicit that this is how a documentation field whose values come from a controlled list is meant to be handled, rather than by inventing classes. Where the ground is statutory and you want to name the instrument rather than just the category, add P17 was motivated by -> the legislation or the clause of the schedule (P17 'describes an item or items that are regarded as a reason for carrying out the instance of E7 Activity'). Where the ground is curatorial, the reason is the officer's own judgement, which is already carried by the E17 itself and its P14.

4. If the outcome is destruction and it is executed, that is E6 Destruction with P13 destroyed -> the file, instantiated jointly with E7 Activity (the E6 scope note: 'Intentional destruction can be documented by classifying the event as both an instance of E6 Destruction and of E7 Activity'), so it can carry P14 carried out by and P17 was motivated by -> the E17 review that authorised it. Destruction under a disposal decision is the single most consequential fact in a record's history and the CRM has a purpose-built class for it.

WHAT DOES NOT (leave it in the records-management system)

The next review date does not belong in the CRM. It is a date attached to an event that has not happened, and the SIG has ruled on this repeatedly and consistently:

- The CRM's overall scope is 'the curated, factual knowledge about the past at a human scale', and from the earliest SIG minutes the model has been described as 'focussed on information about the past, not the future'.
- Asked in 2005 for exactly this pattern under the heading 'Scheduled Treatment', the SIG recorded that 'No construct in CIDOC CRM currently makes it possible to account for an event that has not happened yet.'
- Issue 166 ('New class: "Activity Plan" IsA E29 Design or Procedure') settled it formally at the 22nd meeting in December 2010: because the notion of identity of future events is unclear, 'dealing with instances of E4 in the future (if they exist at all) will be subject of extensions of the CRM, and not part of the scope of CRM.'
- The plan machinery was then pushed out of CRMbase entirely. Issue 333 put 'socExx Activity Plan' and a 'New class socExx Event Specification (of future event)' into CRMsoc; Issue 419 then made it a standalone extension, CRMact v0.2, precisely because it is 'a construct focussing on possible future events rather than past events'. CRMsoc itself was later discontinued (Issue 557, Bern, April 2025). So there is no released, normative CRM class for a scheduled future review, and the archive of this search system carries no labelled declarations for the CRMsoc/CRMact identifiers.

There is a second, independent reason: a due date exists to drive a work queue, and the specification places 'Information required solely for the administration and management of cultural institutions' outside the Intended Scope. A tickler date is administration; the review it triggers, once performed, is history.

PRACTICAL ADVICE

Keep the retention schedule, the calculated next-review date and the review queue in the EDRMS / records-management system, which is built for prospective workflow and for deleting a date once it is superseded. Push into the CRM only what has happened: each completed review as an E17, its date, its officer, the schedule it applied (P33 -> E29), the category assigned, the ground, and any destruction (E6+E7). Note that the E29 retention schedule is the shared object between the two systems - it is a real document that both can point at, which is the natural join.

If you are forced to carry the next review date in the CRM store anyway (for round-tripping), the SIG's own recorded fallback from 2005 is the honest one: an E7 Activity carrying the date as P3 has note, flagged as a plan, not as a dated E52 Time-Span on a temporal entity - a Time-Span asserts the temporal extent of something that exists, and the review does not yet.

One caveat on the object of all this. The CRM distinguishes the physical file from its information content sharply, and archival systems usually do not; note that P13 destroyed takes an E18 Physical Thing, so destruction applies to the paper file, while the 'kept permanently for historical value' judgement is often really about the content. Decide which you are classifying before you instantiate, otherwise the two readings will collide in the same graph. Martin Doerr's framing of what makes an archival institution distinctive - 'the mandate to safeguard records of another institution about their actions' - is the reason this distinction bites harder here than in a museum.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: A disposal review is collection management, so E87 is tempting, but the CRM quantifies P147 curated (E87 -> E78 Curated Holding) as necessary: E87 takes the holding as its object and forces the fonds to be modelled as an E78. It also has no property for recording which retention category was assigned to which file. If the archive wants to place the review inside its curation history, instantiate the E17 jointly with E87 rather than replacing E17 with it.

Usable, and it is E17's parent, so nothing is lost logically. But E17 Type Assignment is the exact specialisation for classifying an item against a controlled category and its scope note names the two things this case needs - the classifier's personal opinion and the date of classification. Using the parent where the child fits loses query precision for no gain.

rejected_alternatives.option: E30 Right for the statutory retention requirement
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E30 is limited to 'legal privileges concerning material and immaterial things', and the SIG's revised scope note in Issue 115 reads 'legal privileges to use material and immaterial things and their derivatives'. A statutory duty to keep a file is an obligation on the holder, not a privilege it enjoys. The SIG's candidate class for obligations (socExx Business Obligation, Issue 557) was never released and CRMsoc was discontinued in April 2025, so there is no CRM class for a statutory duty; record the ground as an E55 Type and point at the instrument with P17.

rejected_alternatives.option: E14 Condition Assessment for the disposal review
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E14 is the act of assessing an object's state of preservation. A disposal review assesses evidential and historical value against a schedule, not physical condition, and its outcome is a retention category rather than an E3 Condition State.

rejected_alternatives.option: E52 Time-Span (via P4) for the next review date
rejected_alternatives.why_not: P4 has time-span attaches a temporal extent to an E2 Temporal Entity, i.e. to something that occurred. The next review has not occurred, and Issue 166 excluded future instances of E4 Period from the scope of the CRM. Modelling the due date this way asserts a phenomenon that did not happen.

rejected_alternatives.option: CRMsoc socExx Activity Plan / socExx Event Specification (of future event)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: These are the constructs the SIG designed for exactly this need (Issue 333), but they were moved out of CRMsoc into a standalone CRMact v0.2 (Issue 419) and CRMsoc was discontinued (Issue 557). They are not part of any released normative model, and this search system holds no labelled declarations for them - the CRMsoc identifiers it does hold are marked historical with no labels. Recommending them would be recommending a moving target.

siblings_considered.why_not: E14 Condition Assessment, the other E13 subclass an archivist would reach for, assesses 'the state of preservation of an object during a particular period'. The disposal review makes no statement about the file's physical condition; it assigns a retention category on grounds of statute or historical value, so E17's classified/assigned pair is what is needed.

E31 Document, the sibling under E73, comprises 'identifiable immaterial items that make propositions about reality'. A retention schedule does not assert facts about the world; it prescribes what shall be done to files of a given class after a given interval. That is E29's definition - documented plans for the execution of actions - and only E29 is the range of P33 used specific technique, which is how the review cites the schedule it applied.

E90 Symbolic Object, the sibling under E28, would treat 'statutory requirement' and 'historical importance' as symbol strings. The case needs them as concepts drawn from a two-term controlled vocabulary that can be queried across files and linked with P127 has broader term; E55 Type is the class the CRM defines for terms from thesauri and controlled vocabularies.

E81 Transformation, the sibling under E64, applies when destruction coincides with the production of new items that preserve recognisable substance from the originals. Shredding or pulping a case file leaves nothing the archive continues to document, so the E6 scope note's own test applies: 'If the matter remaining from the destruction is not documented, the event is modelled solely as an instance of E6 Destruction.'

notes:
in_scope is true but the case is genuinely half in and half out: the disposal-review decision, the schedule it applied and any resulting destruction are squarely modellable; the next review date is not, and I have said so rather than stretching E52 or E7 to cover it.

The search system handled this well in one respect and badly in another. The decision record was excellent: issues 166 -> 338 -> 333 -> 419 -> 557 form a clean twenty-year trail on future events and plans, and the minutes carried the reasoning that the issue pages only summarise. The undocumented --json flag was what made the minutes usable at all - plain `docs` truncates every hit to about 300 characters, which is too short to read an argument, and it prints no chunk ids, so there is no way to move from a `docs` hit to a `quote` verification without first re-running the same query with --json. That should be the default output.

The family models were the weak point. `concept` claims to cover them, and it does for CRMsci/CRMdig/CRMinf/CRMarchaeo/LRMoo/CRMtex/CRMgeo, but CRMsoc is present only as seven unlabelled identifiers (SO1-SO5, SO7, SO17) marked historical, and CRMact is absent entirely. Since Issue 419 makes CRMact the one model in the family that addresses future-oriented constructs, I could confirm from the decision record that it exists and what it is for, but could not inspect a single one of its classes. I have therefore described what the SIG decided rather than proposing CRMact constructs I have not seen.

I found no SIG discussion of archival appraisal or retention scheduling as such. The nearest the mailing list comes is t1306 on whether archivists should adopt the CRM or RiC, which is about description rather than disposal. The mapping onto E17/E29/E6 is mine, argued from the scope notes and the Monotonicity principle, not something the SIG has ruled on.
